mcq.q: Architecture is best described as:
o: The set of decisions that are expensive to change later
mcq.e: Ask how expensive it would be to change in week 10.

mcq.q: Which is an architectural decision?
o: SQL or NoSQL for our data
mcq.e: Where business rules live, framework choice, frontend-backend communication are also architectural.

mcq.q: 'Architecture exists whether you plan it or not.' Unplanned architecture is:
mcq.e: Unplanned just means accidental.

mcq.q: Where does architecture happen in the SDLC?
o: Begins early and continues through implementation, testing and maintenance
mcq.e: The design box is where it is most concentrated, not contained.

mcq.q: The main problem with big up-front design is:
o: Many decisions are made before enough knowledge exists, and feedback arrives late
mcq.e: The failure mode is pretending early guesses are certain.

mcq.q: In incremental design which decisions stay up front?
o: Language, framework, data-model style, system boundaries
mcq.e: Everything else is decided per increment.

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the four forces shaping a trade-off?
mcq.e: The fourth is change: what is most likely to change.

mcq.q: Non-functional requirements:
mcq.e: Functional requirements shape features.

mcq.q: 'Support 10,000 concurrent users' is a:
mcq.e: It describes how the system should behave.

mcq.q: Why is a 1,000,000-user system's architecture more complex than a 500-user one with identical features?
o: The NFRs forced every new box
mcq.e: Load balancers, replicas and caches come from NFRs.

mcq.q: A requirement is an architectural driver if:
o: Changing it would change your diagram
It is first in the list
mcq.e: Ask if it doubled or vanished would the diagram change.

mcq.q: Which is most likely an architectural driver?
o: A payment must never be recorded twice
mcq.e: It forces consistency and idempotency design.

mcq.q: Domain-first design starts from:
o: The concepts of the problem (student, course, enrolment ...)
mcq.e: Technology-first gives a pile of tools.

mcq.q: The pipeline from domain to components is:
mcq.e: Name components after the problem.

mcq.q: Customer, Order and Payment could be:
o: Either modules in a monolith or microservices, depending on trade-offs
mcq.e: Do not mirror every noun as a service.

mcq.q: For the Order concept, 'calls Payment' is best:
mcq.e: Notifying the restaurant is async via a queue.

mcq.q: POST /orders, GET /orders/42, PATCH /orders/42/status are the ___ of the Order concept.
mcq.e: The API was hiding inside the domain analysis.

mcq.q: Low coupling means:
o: You can change one thing without breaking five others
mcq.e: Every arrow is a way for a change to spread.

mcq.q: A UserService with login, invoice, email, tax, report and payment has:
mcq.e: Six unrelated jobs.

mcq.q: A Student class that saves to SQL, sends email and renders HTML violates:
mcq.e: Four jobs, four reasons to change.

mcq.q: Adding a new payment method as a new class implementing PaymentMethod follows:
mcq.e: Extension without editing tested code.

mcq.q: CashOnDelivery extends Payment with a refundToCard that throws. Which principle is broken?
mcq.e: A subclass must not lie about the parent's promise.

mcq.q: Injecting a Repository interface into RegistrationService illustrates:
mcq.e: Production MySQL, tests in-memory, swap with one line.

mcq.q: YAGNI means:
mcq.e: Build for the requirements you have.

mcq.q: When should you add an interface according to the lecture?
o: When two implementations exist today (feel the coupling first)
mcq.e: One hypothetical future one is not a reason.

written.q: What makes a decision architectural? Give two architectural and two implementation decisions.
written.a: An architectural decision is one that is expensive to change later (test: how costly would it be to change in week 10?). Architectural: SQL vs NoSQL; where the business rules live; how the frontend talks to the backend; which framework. Implementation: name of a private method; for vs while; list vs dictionary; button colour.

written.q: Explain why non-functional requirements shape architecture, using the 500-user vs 1,000,000-user example, and what an architectural driver is.
written.a: The same features need one server and one DB for 500 users but load balancing, several app servers, a cache and a primary/replica DB for 1M users at 24/7, under 2 s and 99.9 % availability. The NFRs forced every extra component. An architectural driver is a requirement whose change would change the architecture diagram (e.g. 10,000 orders per minute); a PDF export or button text is not.

written.q: Describe the method for going from a problem domain to system components and unfold the Order concept.
written.a: Problem domain, then identify entities and concepts, responsibilities, relationships and finally system components. For Order: component OrderService; data orders(id, customerId, restaurantId, status, total, placedAt); API POST /orders, GET /orders/42, PATCH /orders/42/status; interactions: synchronous call to Payment, asynchronous notification to the restaurant, an OrderPlaced event.

written.q: Explain SOLID with a project-scale example for each principle and explain YAGNI.
written.a: SRP: split OrderManager into ordering, pricing, payment, mailing and analytics classes. OCP: PaymentMethod interface so new methods are new files. LSP: CashOnDelivery must honour Payment's contract (use Refundable). ISP: small Printable/Scannable/Faxable instead of OfficeMachine. DIP: inject a Repository so MySQL, in-memory test or Postgres can be swapped. YAGNI: abstractions cost, so add them when coupling hurts, not for hypothetical futures.
